utterances.text: Well, we have your statement. I'm not going to take time over it. It is accepted that in that statement you did, page 6 of the statement, give a description. Do you follow? You can look it up yourself if you wish. Page 6 at the bottom, page 7 at the top or 00032181. Second paragraph -- well, second main paragraph down. Do you have it? Should I give you the longer number? Would that be easier? I'll do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, he's reading a different language than you so the exact pagination will not be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that. I'm much obliged. Well, it's -- I haven't got the original-language statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you find, please, the paragraph in the original language where you say: "I didn't pay attention to the different soldiers in the camp except for a few that I recall. One was clearly the Commander of the camp."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I may help, it's at the bottom of the page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. I've just been handed it as well. Yes, much obliged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bottom of page 5 in the Serbian. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you kindly explain why you did not tell the investigator that this exception that you remember, the commander, was somebody you had seen on possibly hundreds of occasions, either on television or on the Internet?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I didn't mention that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were interviewed by the investigator, did he show you a photograph of the person who you think was the commander of the place where you'd been in detention?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He merely showed me the photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So according to you, you were not shown a photograph of the man you thought was the commander. Is -- I want to be clear about that. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he didn't show them to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move on. I want to move on to the next stage, which is the rest of 2003 into 2004. Having made the statement - excuse my voice, I have a cold -- having made the statement in January 2003, did you subsequently appreciate that certain people had been arrested in relation to the matter about which you had given a statement?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. After the making of your statement in January 2003, did you become aware that people had been arrested in relation to the matters contained in your statement?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not know that until our arrival here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One further question. Before you came here, did you either see or read or hear about the start of this trial in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard that there was a trial going on, but we didn't know if it concerned us. We had a very general idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in the habit of using your computer regularly and receiving daily news about Kosovo, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would have been interested to know when the trial started and what was being said about the very things you'd spoken about in your statement, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the other microphone for the witness be switched on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the newspapers it only said that the trial began, but there was no other information, just some general information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any names of defendants given in the newspapers you read?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you had watched television and seen the Internet with the photograph we've been talking about, was a name ever mentioned on television in relation to that photograph?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about your arrival here and you mentioning this photograph on the Internet for the first time. That's what I want to ask you about. Would it be fair to say that before arriving here you had not told anyone from the ICTY that you had seen this photograph many times on the Internet. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be fair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having arrived here on Saturday the 27th of November, you've already indicated there was a proofing session, as it's called, and you didn't mention it then. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On Sunday, the 28th, there was another proofing session and you didn't mention it then. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It isn't right?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't mention it, sorry. Why didn't you mention it on these first two proofing sessions?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wasn't thinking about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given your statement of January to read?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you carefully, therefore, as you've indicated today, that the occasion on which you did mention it was the second session with Mr. Nicholls. So we have a date. The second session with Mr. Nicholls was on Wednesday, the 1st of December; in other words, not long ago, last week.

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did it come about on this second session, not the first, with Mr. Nicholls that for the first time you remembered this photograph?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked me -- he read out his [as interpreted] statement where the name of the [Realtime transcript read in error: "photograph"] commander was indicated, and then he just remembered that his photograph was on the Internet and that it had also been on the news.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask for care about this. What has come up on our screens is that "He asked me -- he read out" -- I think it should be the -- I think you said "his statement," in fact. His statement where the name of the photograph was indicated. He remembered that his photograph was on the Internet and that it had also been on the news. Now, that's what's been recorded and I want to ask you about that answer. What statement did you read out, or did Mr. Lehtinen read out or Mr. Nicholls, as he's the one doing this session, Mr. Nicholls read out where the name of the photograph was indicated?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: He read out my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But your statement doesn't have the name of the photograph being indicated, does it?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what do you mean about the statement being read out where the name of the photograph was indicated?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name was never mentioned because I didn't know his name. He merely asked me to explain, or rather to describe what the man that others referred to as the commander looked like. And then I said that it would be easier to have a look at the photograph because his photograph was on the Internet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had already given a description of the man who you say was the commander in your statement, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was problem?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean the problem?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Nicholls indicate why he was asking you a lot more questions about a description you'd already given?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never said why. He just went through my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ask you why you'd never mentioned this before, that is, the photograph on the Internet?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He didn't? Was the description you gave of the commander the same as the description you gave in your statement? The one you gave to Mr. Nicholls, was it the same?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mention to Mr. Nicholls that the man you remember as the commander had longer gray hair?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because that's not how you describe it in your statement, is it? And you can look at it again if you wish, page 5 at the bottom. Do you appreciate the difference between what is in the statement and what you were telling Mr. Nicholls and of course what you've told this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Maybe in fairness to the witness, he could be read what he actually said in his direct testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- which is -- if he could just be read that rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Certainly. I will read both if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in your statement if you just follow it kindly: "He was fairly tall, 185 to 190 centimetres, black hair, and was usually unshaved." Just dealing with that for the moment. You didn't indicate to the investigator originally in that statement that he had longer graying or gray hair, did you?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say he had longer graying hair, but that he had gray hair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Gray hair.

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is difference between long and gray.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm actually more interested at the moment in the colour. Did this commander who you saw at the camp or however it's described, did he have gray hair then?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you just -- as you talk about length, just tell us what you remember about its length, please, the length of the hair of the person who you say was the commander at the camp.

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looked as if he hadn't had a haircut for a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of months' growth. Would you kindly look around the court, and if there's no objection indicated, if there's anyone in the court whose length of hair resembled -- not the colour, just the length of hair -- resembles the length of hair you remember on the commander. Is there anyone in this room?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little longer than yours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little longer than mine. Now, the commander in the camp, did he have facial hair or a beard, however described?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was unshaven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was unshaven. Yes. Did he have a beard, facial hair?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean exactly. He was simply unshaven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to put to you what you said last Friday. Do you remember what you told this Tribunal about his facial hair?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did I say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's not the question. I'm sorry. Do you remember what you said on Friday about his facial hair?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was unshaven, that he had not shaved for some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm now going to read to you, and I can give the page and so forth if it's required: Day 14, page 11, line 7 to 8. The question you were asked was: "And did he have any facial hair?" Your answer was: "No. He was clean-shaven, not freshly shaven, but he didn't have any facial hair." Now, that's what you said on Friday. Is that description that you gave on Friday accurate?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think it is. The man in the photograph on television that you had seen many times and on the Internet possibly hundreds of times, did the man in the photograph have a beard or facial hair? Or was he unshaven? Shaven? Or what was the position of the man in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not freshly shaven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a beard, the man in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a little, because he had not shaved for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were being asked questions by Mr. Nicholls, did he point out to you that in fact the investigator in January 2003 had shown you a photograph of the commander alleged?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Nicholls didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to consider this for a moment. You have said clearly that you were not shown a photograph of the commander as you remember it, the man in the photograph on the Internet, by the investigator in January 2003. Do you remember saying that today, twice?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could he be shown, please, and I would like it to become an exhibit, B1, which is by reference 00032189.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We have a colour copy which -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, I'd be much obliged if the colour copy could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's semi-colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want it on the ELMO, Mr. Mansfield?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, please. Then it's easier for everyone to see that we've got the same photograph. Hopefully it's the same one, same line-up anyway. B1. It should be a photo line-up, B1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That man is not on the photograph, I mean the same person who is on the Internet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, the Chamber does not presently have a colour version of B1. I think if it's to be an exhibit that would be of some significance, because the black and white photocopies we have are no where near as useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I believe mine is a colour version. I'm happy to hand this one in. I'll just take a label off it. Yes, I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could it become DL1 as I understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, that will be Defence Exhibit DL1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski. Cross-examined by Mr. Topolski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I represent a man called Isak Musliu and I just have a few questions for you. I want to ask you first of all, please, about your attitude as an 18 year old, very nearly 19, in the summer of 1998, your attitude toward the KLA. Could you summarise what that was in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we were told afterwards in school appeared on TV, just like every other Serb child I had the same opinion, that they were not good towards the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your evidence on the 3rd of December, last week in other words, you described them as "terrorists." Would that be your opinion of the KLA, terrorists?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what everybody called them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that's what everybody called them. I'm asking you of your opinion of them. Would you agree that they were terrorists?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is my personal opinion important at this point? I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can assure you that if objection had been taken to my question, or any Judge of this Chamber felt that it was inappropriate to ask you this question, I would have been interrupted by now. So I'll ask you once more and then I shall move on. Did you think of the KLA in the summer of 1998 as terrorists?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know in the summer of 1998 of a place called the State Security Centre?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know in the summer of 1998 of the names of David Gajic and Dragan Jasevic, both men connected to the State Security Centre?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked last week about interviews and meetings that you had with members of the Serbian authorities. Do you remember a large number of questions were asked of you last week about that subject?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to those questions asked of you by Mr. Guy-Smith predominantly - exclusively, in fact - you'd told us that you'd met with Serb investigators two or three times after your release from the camp. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of those meetings, you told us, was at the Red Cross premises in Pristina and Ruzica Simic was present as well. Do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serb investigators say that your mother had been on the television while you had been held?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether they said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say that they knew that Sergeant Genov had been taken as well?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the name Genov mentioned at all by them during any of your meetings with them, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked to look at any maps or plans or drawings of the place where you had been held?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you shown any photographs by the Serb authorities of the place where you had been held?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for your father, I only want to ask you two questions about the events in the place themselves. I can take the first one very shortly. In your own witness statement, you estimate the number of soldiers you saw at this place as around 50. Do you remember saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, all this time later, does the figure "around 50" match your memory of the number of soldiers you would have seen at the place where you were held?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how many of them I saw. They took turns constantly. They were changing. I didn't count them, but that would be my approximation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well I'll settle certainly for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to deal with the photograph, the now rather familiar photograph we've been looking at with other witnesses. I see it's now 2 minutes before 25 past. Would you like me to finish this topic or not start it before the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have further topics?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to put the photograph and deal with that. Your Honours have seen me do this exercise before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm just asking whether that will be the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I have one other, apart from that. And that will be it. And none of it will take long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why don't you carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a photograph, but before I do I want to ask you this: A number of the soldiers or people at the place wore masks, did they not?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the subject of masks and of uniforms, I'd like you to look at a photograph, please, and it's P18, a photograph we have looked at before. Now, I should tell you straightaway, it's not being suggested by me that there is anyone here that you would recognise. This is just a sample. Do you understand? Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look carefully, I think you'll see five masked individuals, three of them standing, two of them seated, in this group of people.

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking only at the masks, I think you might agree with me, sir, that four of them have a mask of a similar style; one of them has a mask of a slightly different style in terms of the area around the eyes. First of all, do you agree with what I've just suggested to you?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First question: As far as any masked individual that you saw during your stay at the place, did any of them wear masks similar to the style of mask we see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: These four individuals wearing the same kind of mask. They looked like that more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that we see, broadly speaking, two different kinds of uniform in this photograph? We see what appears to be a black uniform and we see one gentleman wearing what I shall describe as a camouflage uniform. Do you agree with my descriptions?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Taking it in turn, did you see soldiers wearing camouflage uniform of the type we see the gentleman seated wearing? While you were at the camp of course is what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the black uniform of all of the others, did you see anyone wearing a uniform like that?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll see from the arms of three of them, on the left arm of each appears to be an arm band with the letters, I suggest, "PU." At the camp, did you see anyone in the period you were there, of course, wearing such an armband?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I never saw anyone with this insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again for the sake of completeness, that deals with armbands with PU on it. What about insignias on caps or headwear? Did you see anyone wearing a cap or a hat with "PU" on it as far as you recall?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I ask you about the photograph. I want to deal with just one other topic. You have been asked a lot of questions today about your use of the Internet. I want to understand just two things and then I have two questions. Do I understand your evidence to be that predominantly you visited a web site called www.kosovo.com?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I happen to be interested in Kosovo, yes, that was the site I visited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that you visited other Serbian sites, is that right, web sites?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any information or details posted on any of those web sites from survivor groups or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a long list of survivors and of those who had gone missing. That was all there is -- there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an opportunity to exchange information or get information from any web site in relation to survivors?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell your father of the existence of these web sites?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the answer. I think one of your microphones might be switched off -- it's back on now. The question, Witness, was: Did you tell your father of the existence of these web sites?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell anybody else of the existence of these web sites?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you between the time you got your computer and meeting with investigators in January 2003 the receiver of any e-mail from anyone claiming to be a survivor or connected to any survivor of the war in Kosovo, and in particular the place where you were taken? Did you hear from anyone?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make contact with anyone yourself or try to?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of Serbs and Albanians sharing information regarding Serbs and Albanians? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father ever speak to you about such a thing?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last matter. By my calculation you got here to The Hague around -- on or about the 27th of November and you first began to give evidence before this Tribunal on the 3rd of December.

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Adding together the periods of time you told Mr. Guy-Smith you were in what are known as proofing sessions, if my arithmetic is reliable, which it often isn't, it comes to about eight and a half hours. Would that accord with your memory, sir, some eight and a half hours spent with Prosecutors before giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want any of the detail, even the agenda, still less the name of anyone concerned, but you were -- were you put in touch with something called the Victims and Witnesses section of this Tribunal, people to help you?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: People to whom you could talk, people to whom you could confide any difficulties or problems you may have. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm having a real difficulty seeing how this could possibly be relevant and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Just wait for the next question and you'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Before we get to the next question, I object to the witness having to answer questions about his contacts with Victims and Witnesses and being able to talk about any problems, personal problems he may have had here. Or just ordinary difficulties. These people are translators and are there to help the witness. It's got nothing to do with his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls was too fast to his feet, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you rehearsed by Prosecutors as to what the evidence you were to give in this case? Do you understand what I mean by rehearsed? Let me put it another way. The eight and a half hours you spent with Prosecutors -- not with Victim and Witness section, but with Prosecutors -- did you, you, regard that as a rehearsal?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean. This is the first time that I am in a courtroom. They merely told me what the questioning would look like, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's all I ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will break now. I'm told that for technical reasons a half-hour will be required by the technicians before we can resume with the tapes. So we will resume at 5 past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P80. Re-examined by Mr. Nicholls:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've been asked a lot of questions about that photograph; I want to show it to you one more time. I want you to look at it for me, think. Look at the picture of the man you've indicated with the arrow. Is that the man who was commander in the camp while you were there, while you were held there?

utterances.speaker: (REDACTED) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Sir, you'll be pleased to know that that is the end of your questioning. You are now free to leave The Hague and return to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would like to thank you for your attendance and the assistance that you've given us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been my pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may leave now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I be excused, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you like me to withdraw and find out what's going on outside the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm about to have -- here we are. The next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to take the card and read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I know this is a difficult process for you giving evidence here this evening. I do apologise that you've had to wait so long. Please do relax as best you can. I'm going to ask you a series of questions and just answer them as best you can. And I suspect that your evidence will be finished quite quickly. Are you feeling all right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm right in saying your name is Ljiljana Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were born in 1959?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise for interjecting so early. Just for the record, we do understand and sympathise with the witness. It should be known for the record that all members on this side of the bar were very happy to accept this witness's testimony to be read into evidence or otherwise produced, rather than to require her to attend court. Of course it is a matter for the Prosecution, but as far as our position is concerned, I thought we should make matters clear for Your Honours' attention and information. One again, I apologise for interrupting my learned friend, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just on that issue, I think it may be true in respect to two Defence counsel, but it was indicated to me on Friday, certainly the message was passed to me, that one counsel may, may have questions for this witness. So I merely add that as a point of clarification on what Mr. Khan has just said. If I can continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born in 1959. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were born in Istok in Kosovo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you are a Kosovar Serb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges your level of education.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I am a legal technician. I was educated in two languages, in Albanian and in Serbian. And I have a certificate as an interpreter for Albanian and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm right in saying that until 1998 you had lived all of your life in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are of the Orthodox religion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you were married in 1982. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to whom were you married?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I was married to Slobodan Mitrovic from Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could just be shown a marriage certificate and we'll put that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if -- Mr. Registrar, if I could have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P84.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is my marriage certificate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that your husband Slobodan Mitrovic was from Suva Reka. Just to establish a few points, was he a Serb also?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What languages did your husband speak?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Serbian, Russian, and Albanian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to 1998, am I right in saying that he had lived all of his live in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Mitrovic, you can put that document down now. Thank you. Were there children of your marriage to Slobodan Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have twins, a boy and a girl.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were they born?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: The 13th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you very briefly to think about the time before the war. I think you and your husband ran a company together in Suva Reka. What did that company do?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: A wide range of activities; trade, a private TV channel, a driving school, and an agency that helped you get all the personal documents that you required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the ethnicity of your customers, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: 90 per cent of them were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain why so many Albanians used your company?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all because we were well-respected by them in that area, perhaps even in a wider region; and secondly, 90 per cent of the population there were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any Albanians that worked for your company?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The driving instructors -- in fact, just one, his name was Tefik Kabashi from Gorisha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say 90 per cent of the population where you lived were Albanians. Did you and your husband have any Albanian friends in the area?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to direct your mind to the springtime of 1998. So March, April, May of 1998. Can you think of that period for me?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts were you living at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We lived in Recani. That's a suburb of Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I showed you a map do you think you would be able to point out to the Judges where you lived?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is map 6 of P1. If you could just look at it in front of you for a moment, Mrs. Mitrovic, and see if you can find where you lived --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you place the map on the ELMO. And if you could point out -- so can you just point out to the Judges where you lived.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And just for the record, the witness has indicated with a pointer to the town of Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Mitrovic, did you actually live in Suva Reka itself or did you live outside of it, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We had an apartment in Suva Reka, but we were building our house on the outskirts of Suva Reka, about 2 kilometres from it. We were unable to continue living in our apartment because it was occupied. We had to go and live in the suburbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of that place where you lived in the suburbs?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: The village of Recani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at this particular time can you describe for the Judges what the security situation was like, as you remember, in the Suva Reka area in the spring of 1998.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a difficult time. The children could no longer go to school. There were roadblocks. We couldn't pass them. There were protests practically every day, demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was mounting the roadblocks? Who had put these roadblocks in place, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Probably Albanians, terrorists. Who else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that the reason the children could no longer go to school, because of these roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That was one of the reasons. There is also the other reason. I saw that when I took them to school one day. I came across a group of protesters, thousands of them. They wanted to overturn our car and to kill my children. We barely got out of that situation alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to think of a village above Recani, the village of Budakovo. Do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what was going on in that village at this time, if you can recall.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Nobody -- none of us Serbs could go there. It was quite obvious that columns of trailer trucks were going up there with sand. It was obvious that some construction was going on. We heard later from some farmers, some shepherds, that trenches were being built there and that new roads, macadam roads, were being constructed so that they would not have to use the roads that were already there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was doing this construction work in Budakovo?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you didn't see this construction work with your own eyes, did you?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Not the construction work, but I did see the trailer trucks that transported sand to that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as the other matters that you've stated, that trenches were being dug and roads were being constructed, you heard that from other people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you and your husband feel at this time?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was terrible. You lived for years with another people in love and harmony and all of a sudden these other people puts up barricades. You can no longer go to work. Your children can't go to school. You can't live normally. It's simply terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to direct your mind specifically to the month of May 1998, and I think your husband Boban, Slobodan Mitrovic, was visited by an old Albanian man at his office. Can you recall what your husband told you about that event?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that quite clearly. An old man came to see him. I don't know exactly where he was from, from Seminisa [phoen], from Studencani. At any rate, from the municipality of Suva Reca. He used to be a friend of my father-in-law, Blagoje Mitrovic. He came to see Slobodan, asked him whether he was Slobodan Mitrovic, a son of Blagoje Mitrovic from Recani. When Slobodan confirmed that, he said that he had come there as a friend, that he could not forget all the good that Blagoje Mitrovic had done for the Albanian people in that area and that he felt he had a moral obligation to tell Slobodan, since he had heard that we finally after nine years of marriage got children, that we should take our children somewhere safe to Serbia because there would be a major war there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you and your husband react to this warning?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We couldn't believe this, since we were such good friends with Albanians. We thought that nothing of the sort could happen. We decided not to take our children anywhere, to stay with there our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thinking ahead to the next month, to June, you've already described the security situation for us in Suva Reka. Did matters become better or worse in terms of security?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: It became more and more difficult. The children didn't go to school. That school year was interrupted. The town itself was blocked. We couldn't get out. Anywhere we went, there was a risk involved. It was dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you now that direct your mind to the 14th of June of 1998 and if you can recall what happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We had not had any sleep that night. We didn't sleep that night because there is a forest behind my house and a river and throughout that night we could hear the cars passing through and along the roads that had been opened by the terrorists. We could hear very strange sounds. It sounded like birds. The night was horrible. We simply couldn't fall asleep. We were alone at home with our children and the important thing was not to create panic because of the children. Just before dawn I went to lie down a little bit. I was fully dressed. We had not taken our clothes off, as we had not done before, and just before daybreak my husband came to me and woke me up. He said I should get up quickly. He had been listening to the news and that we were under siege, a blockade, that all the roads were blocked and the only way out is through Brezovica, if that is blocked then there is no way out for us. The question was what to do with children, whether we should take them out, try to save them, or to leave them there. I simply couldn't make that decision. I wanted him to decide and then he wanted me to decide. We simply didn't know what to do. We were supposed to leave our home, our house, the house in which our ancestors had lived for centuries. We simply couldn't bring ourselves to take our children away from the house which we called our home --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you there. Did you in fact eventually make a decision to leave the house in Recani?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Boban reached the decision. He said I should pack the basic things for the children, that we should not sacrifice them after all the trouble that we had gone through to have them. So on the 14th we set out for Serbia via Brezovica. We wanted to go to my parents'.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you, Boban, and the children went to Serbia to be with your parents. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Boban went back right away. He didn't want to leave his area, the country where he had lived for so long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you: Where did Boban go back to?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to repeat the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to have to ask you repeat that. You said Boban went back right away. I'm simply asking you: Where, were did Boban go after he delivered you and the children to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: He went home to Recani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the 15th of June of 1998, did you speak with your husband at all, you being in Serbia and he being in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We spoke every day, sometimes even several times a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your company in Suva Reka continue to function during this time?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. Boban told me that he had let them go home until further notice that so we see what will happen. He said that the peacekeeping forces would come, that perhaps there would not be any war, that things may calm down and that in that case we would come back for me and the children and we would all go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've stated to the Court: "Boban told me he had to let them go until further notice." Who did Boban have to let go home?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: The employees in our company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did he have to let them go home?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Because they could no longer come to work. Everything was blocked. There were roadblocks all over the place and it simply was not safe to travel. The war had practically already started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you next see your husband?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I saw him on the 23rd of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts did you see him?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: In Arandjelovac. He came to us with his aunt's son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Arandjelovac, that is the town in Serbia where you were staying with your parents and the children?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why did your husband appear in Serbia with his cousin?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: He came to fetch the other cousin, Miodrag -- Milovan Krstic who had been in hospital for treatment. They wanted to take him home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me just get this correct with you. Who was Milovan Krstic?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Milovan Krstic is Boban's cousin, his aunt's son, and he's the brother of Miodrag Krstic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so Miodrag Krstic is also your husband's cousin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's also his cousin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your husband appeared in Serbia with Milovan. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did they come to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: They wanted to collect Miodrag from hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was Miodrag in hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to show you some photographs. Where were Milovan Krstic and Miodrag Krstic from?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: From Recani.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown 2166. This is U0032166, Your Honours, from Prosecutor's Exhibit P54. If you can allow the witness to look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I realise this is a relative, but can you just identify that individual for me?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Milovan Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 2167, also from Prosecutor's Exhibit P54.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify that individual for me, Mrs. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Miodrag Krstic, shown on this photograph with his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. You can take those away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Milovan Krstic have a nickname, as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was called Mona.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Miodrag Krstic, did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: He was called Mija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when your husband arrived in Serbia, did you say anything to him about the journey that he was making?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was shocked when I saw him. I said, Goodness, are you normal? And he said, Well, thank you very much for welcoming me. But I had said that because I had seen on TV that the roads had been blocked. So I asked him why he had taken this risk and why he had come. And I also asked him to stay and not to go back until the situation calmed down. He didn't heed my advice, despite the fact that the children pleaded with him as well. They were both of the same opinion, Milovan and Boban; they thought that they should go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "go home," to which place are you referring?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: To Recani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they would go home after collecting Miodrag from hospital in Belgrade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's why they had come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to direct your mind now to the 24th of June of 1998, which is in fact the next day. Can you tell the Judges what you heard from other people took place in respect of your husband, Slobodan, and Milovan and Miodrag Krstic.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I heard they had been kidnapped by terrorists, that they never made it home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can get -- before we get to that point in time, what I'd like you to do is to address the time that they left Belgrade. I know, again, this is what you heard from other people, but if you could address from the time they left Belgrade, what you know of the time up until, as you say, they got kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: They started on the 24th of June. They were going home to Recani from Belgrade after having collected Miodrag Krstic. They called Miodrag's sister from Krusevac and they said they had taken a stop there because Milovan was still very ill and the journey was too taxing for him, but they were in a rush to get home before dark because everybody knew that no one could leave home after dark. It was not safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. Where did Miodrag's sister live?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: She lived in Barajevo in Serbia. It is a suburb of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is she that told you the three of them had called from Krusevac. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. She called me on the phone and told me that they had called, that I should not worry, that they were still in Krusevac, and they would hurry to get home before dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what happened on the rest of that evening, for the remainder of that evening.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We called each other. I called Recani. I inquired whether they had arrived; but they had not. Then I thought that they had stopped in Pristina and they had decided to spend the night there. My first thought was that they called up my uncle, so I called my uncle and asked him if they were there. The answer was negative. He said that they had not called there. Then I thought that they might be gone to a friend's house and that they would continue the journey the next day. The next day I no longer called. I panicked because they had not shown up, and I just didn't know where they were. And I just thought to myself, Oh my God, where are they now? So I thought perhaps I should better call friends from SUP and find out whether the roads had -- were still blocked, whether the car had entered the territory of Kosovo at all. And the answer I got was that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I stop you there? Now, you say that you contacted friends from SUP. You mean that you contacted friends in the police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what information were the police able to give you?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: That a blue Golf carrying three gentlemen had entered the territory of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did that blue Golf belong to, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: This blue Golf bearing Kotor licence plates belonged to Miodrag Krstic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the police, or did you give to the police the number plate of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I knew the number but it was a long time ago. I no longer remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the police confirmed that the particular blue Golf with the licence plates that you stated had crossed the border at a certain time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall where the vehicle crossed the border into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at Merdare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you'd received that information, what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I packed my bag and set out for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you can remember, what sort of date was it that you actually got to Kosovo? Was it the next day? Was it two days later? After June 25th?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: The next day, and I arrived the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go when you got to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Recani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do in Recani?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I went immediately to look for them. I visited my Albanian friends. I wanted to know whether they had heard something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact hear anything about what had happened to your husband and the Krstic brothers?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They told me that they had been stopped at Crnoljevo and kidnapped by terrorists and taken in the direction of Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall who told you that?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the person that told you that?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Abdyl Kryeziu, from Suva Reka. Hamzi's father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any information from any other --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: His father's name was Hamzi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any other information from any other of your Albanian neighbours about what happened to your husband and the Krstic brothers.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From many sources I learned essentially the same story, that is, that they had been kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe you also spoke to a gentleman by the name of Rade Vujevic?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is he Rade Vujevic?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: He is our friend from Kosovo Polje. It's a town not far from Pristina. He is the owner of the Herzegovina Hotel. He told me the story that he had heard from his friend Dusko who used to work at the SUP in Pristina. There Vesel Pintoli from Tumacine [phoen] had come to see him and that he had told him that Boban and the Krstic brothers had been kidnapped and killed, that he had tried to save Boban but he could hardly save himself because at that time they were being killed by Siptari and that he could not -- that they could not be saved. And if it was of any consolation to me, that he had sent me his last regard and that Boban had fallen, after being shot with only one bullet in the forehead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Mitrovic, would you -- do you want to go on or would you like to take a break?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We can go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever try and find this man, Vesel Pintoli, to get to the bottom of this story?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever find him?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No I once tried to go to Tumacine but I only got as far as the entrance to Suva Reka. And at the checkpoint they wouldn't let me through. They said, Do you want to leave orphans behind you? Do you want to leave your children without their mother? Do you really want to sacrifice all this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Dusko, the Serbian police officer, about this piece of information about your husband, the man who had interviewed Vesel Pintoli? Did you ever speak to Dusko?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to direct your mind to November of 1998 and specifically to the 16th of November, 1998, when I believe that the -- or the godfather of your children, Stevan Savic received a telephone call. Can you tell the Judges the content of that telephone call?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember, yes. He was the godfather of my children. He called me at my mother's home. He said he had got my number from a gentleman who spoke with Macedonian dialect. He wanted to know where he could find me because he had a very important message from Boban to convey to me. My cum, the godfather, he was shocked. And he wanted to hear the story from him, but then the man said that he wanted to tell me directly what the message was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to clarify, your -- the godfather of your children had spoken with a gentleman with Macedonian dialect. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what had that man said, the man with the Macedonian dialect, to your -- to the godfather of your children, Stevan Savic?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: He said that Boban had given me the telephone number to call the godfather and that there was an urgent message from Boban to convey to me. And then this godfather he said he would call later, he needed some time to find the phone number. But he actually wanted to call me to find out whether he should give him my number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Savic give the man with the Macedonian accent your telephone number?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did, after I had given him my consent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you then receive a telephone call from this gentleman with a Macedonian accent?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did this gentleman say to you?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I'd gone home immediately to Suva Reka. I gave the number down there because I thought that he would soon be released. And I wanted to be near so I could receive him. And we agreed to speak again that night. It was difficult. It was difficult because it was very risky for me to go to the apartment, because there is a passage to our building and there is a back entrance to the building which had already been under the control of the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Mitrovic, if we could go directly to the conversation that you had with this gentleman. Can you tell the Judges the content of the conversation that you had with the gentleman with the Macedonian accent.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He called me and he said that he was Boban's friend, that he had seen Boban a few days ago, that Boban said, Hello. And that he asked whether his wife -- his mother was still alive and how his children were. I said, I'm sorry, I didn't quite get your name. He said, I didn't give you my name. I asked him where Boban was. His response was, On the other side. Then he told me that we should meet and talk. I replied that he was welcome to come at any time, that he could come to our place and that we would talk. However, he refused to come. He said that he couldn't that -- because his freedom of movement was limited, that he could not cross the border into Kosovo. I was supposed to come to Macedonia, to Skopje to be more precise. It was a bit strange for me. I said that I did not have a passport, that I couldn't cross the border. He then said that I should try and get a passport and he laughed. It was -- he found it strange that I did not have a passport. He obviously knew me quite well. I said that I would try to get a passport and that we would talk the next day. He called me tomorrow -- the next day at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could stop there, Mrs. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours, if this is an appropriate time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Unfortunately the time we can sit has now expired. It will be necessary for the evidence to continue tomorrow. I'm sorry, Mrs. Mitrovic, but we will have to ask you to return tomorrow afternoon when your evidence will continue. We'll adjourn now until tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
